solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Confused situations transgressed more than once? (7,5)

definitions.note: The second definition reads as a verb phrase: lines that have been crossed, several limits overstepped.

blocks.note: the idiom for a muddle where two parties misunderstand each other, from tangled telephone connections
overstepping a limit is going over the line; do it several times and several lines have been gone over

annotation.surface: A puzzled remark about messy situations where someone kept overstepping the mark.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: 'crossed the line' is the idiom for transgressing, so plural crossings give the phrase again.
annotation.definitionFit: Crossed lines are situations of confusion, like a phone call where two conversations get tangled.

entries.clue: Explain appearance of tragic figure in tournament (5,2)

indicators.note: the tragic figure appears in the tournament, so LEAR is set inside CUP

blocks.note: a cup is a knockout tournament, like the FA Cup
King Lear, hero of Shakespeare's tragedy

annotation.surface: A request to explain why a tragic figure turned up at a sporting tournament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tragic figure' points at Shakespeare: Lear is the stock crossword tragedian.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: clearing up a mystery or misunderstanding means accounting for it.

entries.clue: Place for late news? (8,6)

blocks.note: a slot in a newspaper, a regular section of the page
the surface wants breaking stories; 'the late' are the recently dead, and their news is a report of their lives

annotation.surface: A newspaper editor wondering where to put stop-press stories that arrived after deadline.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late news' suggests breaking stories; 'the late' also means the recently dead, and their news goes in the obituaries.
annotation.definitionFit: An obituary column is where a newspaper reports on the late, those who have died.

entries.clue: They help one see small muscles (5)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Something that lets you see tiny muscles, perhaps a magnifying aid in an anatomy class.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One see small muscles' reads as a single phrase; the split comes after 'see'.
annotation.definitionFit: Specs, short for spectacles, are glasses that help the wearer see.

entries.clue: Settled up with a lad? Stop (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' turns PAID upside down to read DIAP

blocks.note: a lad is a boy, a son

annotation.surface: Someone who has settled their account with a young man, then told to halt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop' is the organ stop: a diapason is one of the main foundation stops of a pipe organ. 'Settled up' looks like one phrase but 'up' is the turnaround instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the diapason is one of the pipe organ's foundation stops, a specialist musical sense.

entries.clue: Bars island adopting new name (4)

indicators.note: IS takes N and N into its family, so they sit inside it

annotation.surface: An island that has decided to take a new name, and now keeps people out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bars' looks like a verb meaning prevents; it is the plural noun for pubs.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: places serving drink, with the plural noun hiding behind the verb sense of preventing.

entries.clue: Completely destroy former gallery containing indecent reproduction pictures primarily (9)

indicators.note: a gallery containing pictures has them within its walls, so TATE holds IRP inside it
primarily means in the first place, so take the first letter of each of the three words before it

blocks.note: the Tate, the London art gallery

annotation.surface: A call to wipe out an old gallery for showing indecent prints.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tate is the gallery crosswords reach for; here it wraps round three initials.
annotation.definitionFit: A formal synonym, from the Latin for pulling up by the roots, so nothing is left.

entries.clue: Barman’s preparation perhaps getting the party going (8,3,3)

definitions.note: Both definitions describe an activity, matching the -ing phrase.

blocks.note: the idiom for easing initial awkwardness

annotation.surface: A barman getting things ready as a party warms up.
annotation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal, and 'perhaps' admits that a barman is just one person who might crack ice; the second is the familiar figurative phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Breaking the ice means easing the first awkwardness so a gathering gets going.

entries.clue: Course supporting piano performer (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, LAYER sits under P and holds it up

blocks.note: p = piano, the musical instruction for soft
a course of bricks is a layer

annotation.surface: A course of study that underpins a pianist's performance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests lessons or a meal; it is a layer, as in bricklaying.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym covering both musicians and actors, which the piano in the surface nudges toward.

entries.clue: Cream tea uncovered, with fewer calories? (5)

indicators.note: TEA loses its outside letters, leaving E

blocks.note: lite = low-calorie, as on food labels

annotation.surface: A cream tea made lighter, with the lid off and fewer calories.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cream tea' is a British afternoon treat of scones, jam and clotted cream, which is exactly what hides that 'Cream' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative synonym: the best of a group rises to the top like cream on milk.

entries.clue: Plain French, neutral in translation supplied by a university (2,7)

indicators.note: NEUTRAL is turned into a different form of itself

annotation.surface: A remark that plain French is neutral once a university translates it.
annotation.walkthrough: The French phrase means in its natural state: food served plainly, or a person naked. 'French' in the definition tells you the answer is a French phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Au naturel is French for plain, cooked or served simply.

entries.clue: French writer to get excited about source of Spanish gold (8)

indicators.note: about means around, so ROUSE is wrapped round S
a source is where something starts, so the source of Spanish is its first letter

blocks.note: to rouse is to stir up, excite
Au, the chemical symbol for gold

annotation.surface: A French author getting worked up about where Spain's gold came from.
annotation.walkthrough: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century philosopher and novelist.
annotation.definitionFit: Rousseau was a French-language writer, author of The Social Contract.

entries.clue: Weird small creatures found around wood after temperature dropped (6)

indicators.note: the creatures are found round the wood, so FRY is split to surround EAK
something dropped is let go, so the T is let go from TEAK

blocks.note: T = temperature, the letter that goes

annotation.surface: Strange tiny creatures discovered near the woods after a cold snap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temperature dropped' reads as the weather turning cold; it tells you to remove T from TEAK.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym, with the surface's odd creatures in the woods making it sound like a horror story.

entries.clue: Mostly lie to get to consume hot slice of meat (4,4)

indicators.note: mostly means not all of it, so PORKY loses its last letter
to consume is to swallow, so COP swallows H and holds it inside

blocks.note: PORKY minus its last letter; a porky is a lie, from rhyming slang pork pie = lie
to cop is to get or catch

annotation.surface: A liar who gets to eat a hot piece of meat.
annotation.walkthrough: A porky is British slang for a lie, from rhyming slang 'pork pie'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the chop is a rib cut, and the word itself means a piece chopped off.

entries.clue: Arch-rival cut down, confounded — I will make a row (9)

indicators.note: ARCH-RIVAL loses its last letter
the remaining letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: Someone vowing to cause a scene about a humiliated arch-rival.
annotation.walkthrough: A charivari is a noisy mock serenade, and by extension any din. 'Row' rhymes with cow here, not with go.
annotation.definitionFit: A dictionary sense: originally a mock serenade of pots and pans for newlyweds, now any din or racket.

entries.clue: Constant collection of birds? Not unknown for eggs (6)

indicators.note: AVIARY without the unknown Y

blocks.note: c, the constant for the speed of light
an aviary houses a collection of birds
y, an algebraic unknown, is removed

annotation.surface: A birdwatcher's steady flock, with a remark about eggs.
annotation.walkthrough: Mathematical unknowns are x, y and z; here Y is the one that goes.
annotation.definitionFit: Caviar is sturgeon roe, fish eggs.

entries.clue: Plant in place for divers, like the sea, at first (8)

indicators.note: BLUE goes in front of BELL

blocks.note: a diving bell holds divers underwater

annotation.surface: A plant growing where divers go, down by the sea.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant in' suggests putting something in the ground; 'Plant' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The bluebell is a woodland plant with blue bell-shaped flowers.

entries.clue: Party of ordinary people returning, well in front (6)

indicators.note: returning is going back the way you came, so LAIC is read right to left
well is placed in front, so SO comes before the rest

blocks.note: laic = of the laity, lay people rather than clergy

annotation.surface: A political party of ordinary people coming back, and well in the lead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' tempts toward politics; a social is a party in the gathering sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun use of the adjective: a club or church gathering, the festive sense of party rather than the political one.

entries.clue: Criticism about husband’s routine (6)

indicators.note: about means around, so STICK is wrapped round H

blocks.note: to get stick is to be criticised

annotation.surface: Complaints about a husband's daily habits.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive but means 'is'. A shtick is a comedian's routine, from Yiddish.
annotation.definitionFit: A shtick is a performer's standard routine or gimmick.

entries.clue: Sensitive French not initially accepting quantity of work (8)

indicators.note: not there at the start, so GALLIC loses its first letter
to accept something is to take it in, so ALLIC takes ERG inside

blocks.note: the erg is a unit of work in physics

annotation.surface: A touchy Frenchman reluctant to take on any work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sensitive French' looks like a description of a person; the definition is 'Sensitive' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Allergic means sensitive to a substance, reacting badly to it.

entries.clue: Just a small amount? Church never accepting raising of tax (7)

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so NO takes TAV inside
in a down clue, raising a word lifts it bottom to top, so VAT reads TAV

blocks.note: VAT, value added tax, the British sales tax

annotation.surface: A church refusing ever to accept a tax rise, as just a small matter.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as by example: a centavo is a hundredth of a peso and many other Latin American currencies.
annotation.definitionFit: A centavo is a small coin, a hundredth of the main unit, so it is only a small amount of money.

entries.clue: Old film story involving King and I? (6)

indicators.note: a story involving characters has them inside it, so TALE wraps round K and I

annotation.surface: An old film about a king and I, echoing the musical The King and I.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark nods to The King and I, itself an old film; you just take K and I literally.
annotation.definitionFit: A talkie was an early film with synchronised sound.

entries.clue: Long broadcast taking hours in review of brief communication (8)

indicators.note: the reversed word takes H inside
NOTELET is looked back over, so read backwards

blocks.note: a notelet is a small folded card for a short note

annotation.surface: A marathon programme that spends hours reviewing a short message.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Review' signals looking back, so NOTELET runs right to left before H goes in.
annotation.definitionFit: A telethon is a very long television broadcast, usually raising money for charity.

entries.clue: Licked? No bit of blancmange consumed (5)

indicators.note: no bit of blancmange means none of it is present, so the B is taken out of BEATEN

blocks.note: first letter of blancmange, which goes

annotation.surface: A child asked whether the plate was licked clean, with none of the blancmange eaten.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Licked' pretends to be about eating; in the wordplay it means defeated. Blancmange is a set milk pudding.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past participle, matching the surface's talk of a pudding finished off.

entries.clue: Long, elegant, but topless (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so S goes

annotation.surface: A description of a long, elegant gown that happens to be topless.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for a dress; it is the verb, to yearn.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: yearning for something, with the adjective sense of length as the disguise.

entries.clue: Bell tower old man placed between rivers (9)

indicators.note: PA sits between the two rivers

blocks.note: the Cam, the river through Cambridge

annotation.surface: A bell tower where an old man lives, standing between two rivers.
annotation.walkthrough: One word, 'rivers', supplies both CAM and NILE.
annotation.definitionFit: A campanile is a free-standing bell tower, from the Italian for bell.

entries.clue: Russian forests end abruptly beside Georgia (5)

indicators.note: ending abruptly means stopping short, so TAIL is cut before its last letter
beside means next to, so GA is placed right after TAI

blocks.note: GA, the postal code for the US state

annotation.surface: Russian forests stopping suddenly at the border with Georgia.
annotation.walkthrough: Georgia the country borders Russia, which is the picture; the wordplay uses the US state's abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: The taiga is the vast coniferous forest of Siberia and northern Russia.

entries.clue: The writer’s recalled challenge distressed old artist (12)

indicators.note: I'M is called back, reading MI
CHALLENGE is knocked out of shape

annotation.surface: A writer upset at being called back to answer a challenge to an old artist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The writer's' is 'the writer is', I'M, not a possessive.
annotation.definitionFit: Michelangelo was the Renaissance painter and sculptor of the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
